topics.title: How Robots See in the Dark
topics.hook: Self-driving cars don't use cameras to see. They use something far stranger.
topics.curiosity_angle: LiDAR — the laser that maps the world 10 million times per second
topics.script: Self-driving cars don't use cameras to see. They fire 10 million laser pulses every second and listen for the echo. That's LiDAR. Each pulse hits an object and bounces back in nanoseconds. The car builds a 3D map of the world — in real time — faster than your eye can blink. Rain, fog, and darkness don't matter. Lasers don't care. This is how robots see. Follow R2BOT to learn the tech shaping the future.

topics.title: PID Controller
topics.hook: Three letters control almost every machine on the planet. P. I. D.
topics.curiosity_angle: The 80-year-old algorithm still running your thermostat, drone, and Tesla
topics.script: Three letters control almost every machine on Earth. P. I. D. Proportional. Integral. Derivative. Your thermostat uses it. Your drone uses it. Your Tesla uses it. A PID controller asks three questions every millisecond: How wrong am I right now? How long have I been wrong? How fast am I getting more wrong? The answers become a correction signal. It's 80 years old — and nothing better has replaced it. Follow R2BOT. Learn the classics.

topics.title: SLAM — How Robots Map Unfamiliar Places
topics.hook: Drop a robot in an unknown room. How does it know where it is?
topics.curiosity_angle: SLAM solves a chicken-and-egg problem that stumped engineers for decades
topics.script: Drop a robot in a room it's never seen. How does it know where it is? This is the SLAM problem. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping. The robot must build a map while using that same map to navigate. It's a chicken-and-egg problem that stumped roboticists for decades. Today, your robot vacuum solves it. So does every autonomous drone and self-driving car. Follow R2BOT — and learn how robots find their way.

topics.title: What is ROS2?
topics.hook: Every serious robot on Earth runs the same operating system. You've never heard of it.
topics.curiosity_angle: ROS2 — the invisible plumbing behind Boston Dynamics, NASA, and every robotics startup
topics.script: Every serious robot on Earth runs the same operating system. You've never heard of it. It's called ROS2. Not Windows for robots — it's the plumbing that lets a robot's parts talk to each other. Quick one. A robot's camera, brain and wheels — one big program, or separate programs? Separate. Each part is a node. The camera is one, the motors another. Independent programs. Nodes never call each other. One publishes to a topic, others subscribe. The camera shouts; whoever cares listens. So you can unplug the camera node, drop in a better one, and nothing else changes. So if one node crashes mid-mission, what happens to the robot? It keeps running. That isolation is why ROS2 is trusted on hardware that can't fail. Free, open source, and the most employable robotics skill there is. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: How Robots Learn to Walk
topics.hook: Nobody taught this robot to walk. It fell over ten million times and worked it out.
topics.curiosity_angle: Reinforcement learning — the same technique that beat world champions, now teaching machines to move
topics.script: Nobody taught this robot to walk. It fell over ten million times and worked it out. That's reinforcement learning. You don't write instructions. You write a reward, and let the machine discover what earns it. Before I explain — ten million falls. On a real robot, or somewhere else? Somewhere else. In simulation, where a robot falls a million times an hour and never breaks a joint. Each attempt gets a score. Moved forward? Points. Face-planted? Penalty. It keeps whatever nudged the score up. Nobody ever defined walking. Walking is just the strategy that scored highest. So what's the hardest part of reinforcement learning? Writing the reward. Reward speed alone and it learns to fall forward — fast, and useless. Teach a machine what to want, and it works out how. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: Degrees of Freedom
topics.hook: Your arm can reach the same cup a hundred different ways. Most robots can't.
topics.curiosity_angle: Degrees of freedom — why six joints is the magic number, and seven is the luxury one
topics.script: Your arm can reach the same cup a hundred different ways. Most robots can't. That's degrees of freedom — how many independent ways a thing can move. A standard robot arm has six. Quick call. To put an object anywhere, at any angle — do you need three, or six? Six. Three to get there: left-right, forward-back, up-down. Three more to aim it: roll, pitch, yaw. With fewer, there are poses it simply cannot reach. A four-joint arm touches the point, but not from your angle. Your arm has seven. That spare one is why you can hold your hand still and swing your elbow around it. So why do surgical robots often use seven joints, not six? To dodge obstacles. The extra freedom reroutes the arm around your ribs without moving the instrument. More freedom, more cost, more control. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: How Robots Recognize Your Face
topics.hook: Your phone recognises you in twenty milliseconds. It has never once seen a face.
topics.curiosity_angle: Computer vision — how a grid of numbers becomes recognition, one layer at a time
topics.script: Your phone recognises you in about twenty milliseconds. And it has never once seen a face. To a machine, an image isn't a picture. It's a grid of millions of numbers — just brightness values. So does it hunt for eyes and a nose, or for something far stranger? Stranger. The very first layer looks for one thing only: edges. Light meeting dark. That's it. The next layer glues edges into corners and curves. The next builds those into eyes and noses. Nobody ever programmed the idea of an eye. The network invented it, by seeing millions of faces and keeping whatever helped. So what does the very first layer of a vision network actually detect? Edges. Only light meeting dark. Every recognisable thing is built on top of that. It learned to see the way you did — from examples. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: How Robots Navigate Obstacles
topics.hook: Your maps app finds the best route in milliseconds. It doesn't check every road.
topics.curiosity_angle: A* — the 1968 algorithm still routing every robot, every game character, and your commute
topics.script: Your maps app finds the best route in milliseconds. And it never checks every road. The trick is A star. An algorithm from 1968 that still routes robots, game characters, and your drive home. So how does it choose? Does it explore every direction equally, or lean toward the goal? It leans. Every option gets scored twice: how far you've already come, plus a guess at how far is left. That guess is the whole idea. Explore the cheapest total first, and you skip huge regions that were never going to win. Checking everything would be perfect but slow. Guessing alone is fast but wrong. A star takes both and stays optimal. What happens if the guess is too optimistic? You lose the guarantee. Overestimate the distance left and A star can confidently return the wrong route. One equation, fifty-eight years, still unbeaten. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: Why Robots Are Strong But Slow
topics.hook: A robot that lifts a car can't move fast. That's not engineering — it's physics.
topics.curiosity_angle: The torque-speed trade-off that decides what every motor on Earth can and cannot do
topics.script: A robot that can lift a car cannot move quickly. That isn't bad engineering. It's physics. Every motor faces the same trade-off: torque, or speed. Turning force, or turning fast. You don't get both. So if you want more force from the same motor — do you make it bigger, or add gears? Gears. A gearbox trades one for the other. Ten times the force out, one tenth the speed. Because power is torque times speed, and the motor's power is fixed. Push one up, the other must come down. That's why a factory arm lifting an engine crawls, and why a drone propeller spins fast but couldn't lift a brick. A gearbox gives you ten times the torque. What's the cost? A tenth of the speed. The energy was never free — you only ever rearranged it. Every robot is a bet on which one mattered more. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: Why Self-Driving Cars Use 5 Sensors
topics.hook: Every sensor on a self-driving car lies. The trick is that they lie differently.
topics.curiosity_angle: Sensor fusion — how several unreliable sensors become one reliable answer
topics.script: Every sensor on a self-driving car lies to it. The trick is that they all lie differently. Cameras miss depth. LiDAR hates fog. Radar is coarse. GPS drifts. Not one of them is trustworthy alone. So which does the car believe? The most accurate one, or all of them at once? All of them — weighted by how much each deserves belief right now. That's sensor fusion. In clear daylight the camera gets a loud vote. In thick fog its vote quietly collapses and radar takes over. The maths behind it is a Kalman filter, and it's older than the Moon landing. Apollo used it to navigate. In heavy fog, which sensor should the car trust most? Radar. Its wavelength sails straight through water droplets that blind both the camera and the LiDAR. No perfect sensor. Just good disagreement. Follow R2BOT.

topics.title: The Hardest Part of a Robot
topics.hook: We can build a robot that runs. We still can't build a hand that picks up a strawberry.
topics.curiosity_angle: The end effector — why the last ten centimetres of a robot are the hardest to engineer
topics.script: We can build a robot that runs and backflips. We still can't build a hand that reliably picks a strawberry. The gripper is called the end effector, and it's where most robotics projects quietly fall apart. So what makes gripping hard — is it the strength, or something else entirely? Something else. It's knowing how hard to squeeze. Too little and it drops. Too much and it's jam. A human hand has thousands of touch receptors correcting grip constantly. Most robot grippers have none at all. So industry cheats. Vacuum cups for boxes, magnets for steel, custom jaws per part. Specialised, not general. Why don't factories just use human-shaped robot hands? Too complex, too fragile, too expensive. A two-hundred-dollar suction cup beats a fifty-thousand-dollar hand. The last ten centimetres are still unsolved. Follow R2BOT.
